Deira
DEER-uh
n. (the southern of the two Northumbrian kingdoms, centred on York and the Yorkshire wolds)
From a British name, perhaps deifr, waters, latinised by Bede as Deira.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Deira was the southern half of Northumbria, the country between the Humber and the Tees with its centre at York, and it was politically distinct from Bernicia to the north for most of the seventh century. Edwin of Deira was baptised at York in 627 by Paulinus and gave the church its first northern see; after Edwin fell to Penda and Cadwallon the kingdom passed under Bernician control, and its last separate king, Oswin, was murdered in 651 at the instigation of Oswiu and buried at Tynemouth. Deira then ceased to exist as a kingdom, though the name survived in Yorkshire place names and in the title of its bishops. The dictionary records Deira because it is a kingdom that vanished within a century of hearing the gospel, which is an ordinary fate for kingdoms and no measure at all of what was done in it. Scripture is content to say that every realm will change hands at last, that the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and that the righteous man rather than the dynasty is the everlasting foundation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a kingdom as the territory of a king; to reign as to possess sovereign power; to destroy as to demolish or ruin; a foundation as the basis of a building; and remembrance as the keeping in mind.

expand to see more

KINGDOM, n. The territory or country subject to a king; dominion; rule; sovereign power.

REIGN, v.i. To possess or exercise sovereign power or authority; to rule; to be predominant.

DESTROY, v.t. To demolish; to pull down; to ruin; to annihilate a thing by demolishing or by burning.

FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; the ground work of any thing; that on which any thing stands.

REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind the idea of a thing which had before been known; honorable memory.

Key Scripture

Rev 11:15 — "And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever."

Dan 2:44 — "And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever."

Pro 10:25 — "As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation."

Psa 112:6 — "Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance."

Modern Corruption

The southern Northumbrian kingdom, centred on York, Christianised under Edwin in 627 and extinguished as a separate realm by 651.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one that makes the extinction of a kingdom bearable: all of them change hands. John hears it announced as a finished fact: “The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ” (Rev 11:15). Daniel had already distinguished the one realm that is not provisional: “And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed” (Dan 2:44).

The live temptation when a people disappears is to conclude that its work disappeared too. Deira lasted barely a generation after Edwin's baptism and gave the north its first bishop, its first stone church and Hild's generation of abbesses. Solomon marks the difference between what the storm takes and what it leaves: “As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation” (Pro 10:25). The Psalter promises the same permanence to persons rather than to realms: “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psa 112:6).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek basileia (G0932), a kingdom; Aramaic malku (H4437), a kingdom; Hebrew suphah (H5492), a whirlwind; Hebrew olam (H5769), everlasting.

expand to see more

Greek basileia (G0932) — a kingdom, a realm; “The kingdoms of this world”, Revelation 11:15.

Greek basileuo (G0936) — to reign; “he shall reign for ever and ever”, Revelation 11:15.

Aramaic chabal (H2255) — to destroy, to corrupt; “a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed”, Daniel 2:44.

Hebrew suphah (H5492) — a whirlwind, a storm; “As the whirlwind passeth”, Proverbs 10:25.

Hebrew olam (H5769) — perpetuity, everlasting; “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance”, Psalm 112:6.

Usage

"“The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord” (Rev 11:15) — every realm, Deira included."

"“a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed” (Dan 2:44) — the one exception."

"“the righteous is an everlasting foundation” (Pro 10:25) — persons outlast kingdoms."
